name: Ford RS200
hook: Ford's Group B supercar was assembled by Reliant, the firm best known for three-wheelers, and one of them held the 0–60 mph world record for twelve years.
story:
Group B had a simple rule. If you wanted to rally a car, you first had to build two hundred for the road.

So Ford designed a rally car and worked backwards. Tony Southgate, a Formula One designer, drew the chassis. Ghia shaped the body. Reliant, better known for three-wheelers, built the road cars at Shenstone.

The layout was odd on purpose. The engine sat behind you. The gearbox sat up front, for better balance. So the power went forward first, then back again to the rear wheels.

Then, in March 1986, an RS200 ran off the road into the crowd in Portugal. By the end of that year, Group B was gone. Ford stopped the road cars and broke many back into parts. Only about 156 were sold complete.

But the best was still to come. Ford built 24 Evolution cars with a bigger 2.1-litre engine. In one of them, the Swedish rally ace Stig Blomqvist reached 60 mph in 3.07 seconds. It was a world record. It stood for twelve years.
description: The RS200 was Ford's purpose-built Group B rally car, and the road version existed to make it legal. It has a mid-mounted 1.8-litre turbocharged Cosworth BDT four, a gearbox at the front and four-wheel drive, under a composite body styled by Ghia. Tony Southgate and John Wheeler designed the chassis, and Reliant assembled the road cars. Group B ended in 1986, before the car could show its full pace, but the 24 Evolution cars and a record 0–60 mph run made its name.
